Prelude — Probability IS Integration

There is a profound unity lurking here:

Every quantity in continuous probability theory is an integral.

Probability itself is an integral. Expected value is an integral. Variance is an integral. Information entropy is an integral. The KL divergence is an integral. The evidence lower bound (ELBO) in VAEs is an integral. The likelihood in a Gaussian process is an integral of an integral.

This is not a coincidence — it is the Kolmogorov foundation: probability is a measure, and computing probabilities of continuous events is Lebesgue integration. For us, working at the level of Riemann integration, the statement is:

P(a≤X≤b)=∫ab​fX​(x),dx​

Every formula in this note is a specialization or composition of this single idea.

The Dictionary:

Probability conceptIntegration concept
Probability of an eventArea under the PDF
Expected valueWeighted area (∫x,f(x),dx)
VarianceSecond central moment integral
IndependenceProduct structure of the joint PDF
ConditioningSlice of the joint, renormalized
Entropy−∫flnf,dx
Generating functionsLaplace/Fourier transform of the PDF

Part I — Foundations

1. Probability Density Functions — The Central Definition

Definition (Rigorous)

A function fX​:R→R is a probability density function (PDF) for a continuous random variable X if:

(i) Non-negativity: fX​(x)≥0 for all x∈R

(ii) Normalization: ∫−∞∞​fX​(x),dx=1

(iii) Probability via integration: P(a≤X≤b)=∫ab​fX​(x),dx

Critical remark: fX​(x) is not a probability. It is a density — analogous to mass per unit length. The probability requires integrating over an interval. P(X=a)=∫aa​fX​(x),dx=0 for any single point. This is conceptually sharp: continuous random variables have probability zero of taking any exact value.

Example 1.1 — Verifying a PDF

Claim: f(x)=ce−3x for x≥0 (and 0 otherwise) is a valid PDF for some c. Find c.

Normalization condition: ∫0∞​ce−3x,dx=1⟹c[−3e−3x​]0∞​=1⟹3c​=1⟹c=3​

Verify: f(x)=3e−3x for x≥0. This is the Exponential distribution with parameter λ=3.

Example 1.2 — Computing a Probability

Setup: fX​(x)=83​x2 for 0≤x≤2. Find P(1≤X≤2).

Step 1 — Verify normalization: ∫02​83​x2,dx=83​⋅3x3​​02​=81​(8)=1✓

Step 2 — Compute: P(1≤X≤2)=∫12​83​x2,dx=83​⋅3x3​​12​=81​(8−1)=87​​

2. Cumulative Distribution Function

Definition & Fundamental Theorem Connection

FX​(x)=P(X≤x)=∫−∞x​fX​(t),dt​

Properties (all derived from the integral):

  • F is non-decreasing (since f≥0, adding more area cannot decrease F)
  • limx→−∞​F(x)=0, limx→∞​F(x)=1
  • F is right-continuous
  • P(a<X≤b)=F(b)−F(a) — this is the FTC for probability

FTC gives back the PDF: fX​(x)=FX′​(x)(almost everywhere)

The CDF and PDF are a FTC pair. PDF is the derivative of CDF; CDF is the integral of PDF.

Example 2.1 — CDF of a Power Distribution

Setup: f(x)=3x2 for 0≤x≤1.

F(x)=∫0x​3t2,dt=t3​0x​=x3,0≤x≤1

Find the median m: F(m)=0.5⟹m3=0.5⟹m=(0.5)1/3≈0.794.

Find the 90th percentile p0.9​: p0.93​=0.9⟹p0.9​=0.91/3≈0.965.

Connection to §9 (Survival/Biology note): The survival function S(x)=1−F(x)=1−x3 gives the probability of exceeding x. Every concept in survival analysis is the CDF or its complement, computed via integration.

Example 2.2 — CDF from a Piecewise PDF

Setup: f(x)={x​0≤x≤1 2−x​1<x≤2 0​otherwise​

(Triangular distribution — note: ∫01​x,dx+∫12​(2−x),dx=21​+21​=1 ✓)

CDF for 0≤x≤1: F(x)=∫0x​t,dt=2x2​

CDF for 1<x≤2: F(x)=F(1)+∫1x​(2−t),dt=21​+[2t−2t2​]1x​=21​+(2x−2x2​−23​)=2x−2x2​−1

Check: F(2)=4−2−1=1. ✓

3. Expected Value & Moments

Definition

For a continuous random variable X with PDF fX​:

E[X]=∫−∞∞​x,fX​(x),dx​

Existence: This integral must converge absolutely — i.e., ∫−∞∞​∣x∣,fX​(x),dx<∞. Some distributions (e.g., Cauchy) have no finite mean because this integral diverges.

Interpretation: E[X] is the center of mass of the distribution — the balance point of the PDF curve. This is literally the same formula as the center of mass integral from the physics note, with fX​(x) playing the role of linear density ρ(x).

Example 3.1 — Expected Value of Power Distribution

Setup: f(x)=(n+1)xn for 0≤x≤1.

E[X]=∫01​x⋅(n+1)xn,dx=(n+1)∫01​xn+1,dx=(n+1)⋅n+21​=n+2n+1​​

Sanity check: As n→∞, the distribution concentrates near x=1, and E[X]→1. As n=0 (uniform), E[X]=21​. Both are correct. ✓

Example 3.2 — Cauchy Distribution Has No Mean

PDF: f(x)=π(1+x2)1​, x∈R.

Attempt to compute E[X]: ∫−∞∞​π(1+x2)x​,dx=π1​⋅21​ln(1+x2)​−∞∞​

This integral diverges (both tails diverge to ±∞). The Cauchy distribution has no finite expected value despite being symmetric about 0.

This is not a mere technicality. In finance, the Cauchy distribution models fat-tailed returns where “the average return” literally does not exist — the empirical mean of samples from a Cauchy distribution never converges, no matter how much data you collect. The divergence of the integral is the mathematics of this phenomenon.

4. Variance, Standard Deviation & Higher Moments

Definition

n-th moment about the origin: μn′​=E[Xn]=∫−∞∞​xn,fX​(x),dx

n-th central moment: μn​=E[(X−μ)n]=∫−∞∞​(x−μ)n,fX​(x),dx

Variance (n=2): Var(X)=E[(X−μ)2]=E[X2]−(E[X])2​

Proof of the shortcut formula: E[(X−μ)2]=∫(x−μ)2f(x),dx=∫(x2−2μx+μ2)f(x),dx =E[X2]−2μE[X]+μ2=E[X2]−2μ2+μ2=E[X2]−μ2■

Skewness (n=3 central moment, normalized): γ1​=σ3μ3​​ — measures asymmetry.

Kurtosis (n=4): γ2​=σ4μ4​​−3 — measures tail heaviness relative to Gaussian.

Example 4.1 — Variance of Triangular Distribution

For the triangular distribution from Example 2.2 with PDF f(x)=x on [0,1] and f(x)=2−x on [1,2]:

E[X] (by symmetry about x=1): E[X]=1.

E[X2]: =∫01​x2⋅x,dx+∫12​x2(2−x),dx=∫01​x3,dx+∫12​(2x2−x3),dx =41​+[32x3​−4x4​]12​=41​+(316​−4)−(32​−41​) =41​+34​−125​=123+16−5​=1214​=67​

Var(X)=67​−12=61​,σ=6​1​≈0.408■

Part II — The Great Distributions, Derived Rigorously

5. Uniform Distribution

PDF: f(x)=b−a1​ for x∈[a,b].

Verification: ∫ab​b−a1​,dx=1. ✓

Mean: E[X]=∫ab​b−ax​,dx=b−a1​⋅2b2−a2​=2(b−a)(b−a)(b+a)​=2a+b​​

Variance: E[X2]=b−a1​∫ab​x2,dx=3(b−a)b3−a3​=3a2+ab+b2​ Var(X)=3a2+ab+b2​−4(a+b)2​=124(a2+ab+b2)−3(a+b)2​=12(b−a)2​​

6. Exponential Distribution

PDF: f(x)=λe−λx for x≥0, λ>0.

Normalization: ∫0∞​λe−λx,dx=λ⋅λ1​=1. ✓

Mean (integration by parts: u=x, dv=λe−λxdx): E[X]=∫0∞​xλe−λx,dx=[−xe−λx]0∞​+∫0∞​e−λx,dx=0+λ1​=λ1​​

Second moment (two integrations by parts): E[X2]=∫0∞​x2λe−λx,dx=λ22​

Var(X)=λ22​−λ21​=λ21​​

Memoryless property (unique to exponential): P(X>s+t∣X>s)=P(X>t)

Proof via integration: P(X>s+t∣X>s)=P(X>s)P(X>s+t)​=∫s∞​λe−λx,dx∫s+t∞​λe−λx,dx​=e−λse−λ(s+t)​=e−λt=P(X>t)■

7. The Gaussian — Derived from First Principles

The Gaussian Integral: Full Proof

Claim: ∫−∞∞​e−x2,dx=π​​

Proof (MIT 18.02 polar coordinate method):

Let I=∫−∞∞​e−x2,dx. Consider I2:

I2=(∫−∞∞​e−x2,dx)(∫−∞∞​e−y2,dy)=∫−∞∞​∫−∞∞​e−(x2+y2),dx,dy

Convert to polar: x=rcosθ, y=rsinθ, dA=r,dr,dθ:

I2=∫02π​∫0∞​e−r2r,dr,dθ=2π∫0∞​re−r2,dr

Substitution u=r2, du=2r,dr:

=2π∫0∞​21​e−u,du=2π⋅21​=π

Therefore I=π​. ■

Corollary: With substitution x=t/(σ2​): ∫−∞∞​e−t2/(2σ2),dt=σ2​∫−∞∞​e−x2,dx=σ2π​

The Normal Distribution

PDF: For X∼N(μ,σ2):

f(x)=σ2π​1​e−2σ2(x−μ)2​​

The normalization constant σ2π​1​ is exactly (∫−∞∞​e−(x−μ)2/(2σ2),dx)−1=(σ2π​)−1, derived above.

Mean: E[X]=∫−∞∞​σ2π​x​e−(x−μ)2/(2σ2),dx

Substitute u=(x−μ)/σ: =∫−∞∞​σ2π​σu+μ​e−u2/2σ,du=2π​σ​=0 (odd)∫−∞∞​ue−u2/2,du​​+μ=1∫−∞∞​2π​1​e−u2/2,du​​=μ​

Variance: Var(X)=∫−∞∞​σ2π​(x−μ)2​e−(x−μ)2/(2σ2),dx

Substitute u=(x−μ)/σ: =σ2⋅2π​1​∫−∞∞​u2e−u2/2,du

Integration by parts: v=u, dw=ue−u2/2,du: ∫−∞∞​u2e−u2/2,du=[−ue−u2/2]−∞∞​+∫−∞∞​e−u2/2,du=0+2π​

Var(X)=σ2⋅2π​2π​​=σ2​

Example 7.1 — The 68-95-99.7 Rule (Exact Integrals)

For X∼N(0,1), using the error function erf(z)=π​2​∫0z​e−t2,dt:

P(−kσ≤X≤kσ)=erf(2​k​)

kP(μ−kσ≤X≤μ+kσ)Exact Integral
1≈0.6827erf(1/2​)
2≈0.9545erf(2​)
3≈0.9973erf(3/2​)

These cannot be expressed in elementary closed form — they require the error function, a non-elementary antiderivative defined by the integral. The Gaussian is the canonical example of a function whose integral is non-elementary but profoundly important.

8. Gamma Distribution

The Gamma Function: An Improper Integral

Definition: Γ(n)=∫0∞​tn−1e−t,dt,n>0​

Key properties derived from integration:

(i) Recursion: Γ(n)=(n−1)Γ(n−1)

Proof: Integration by parts, u=tn−1, dv=e−t,dt: Γ(n)=[−tn−1e−t]0∞​+(n−1)∫0∞​tn−2e−t,dt=0+(n−1)Γ(n−1)■

(ii) Integer values: Γ(n)=(n−1)! for n∈N

(iii) Half-integer: Γ(1/2)=π​

Proof: Γ(1/2)=∫0∞​t−1/2e−t,dt. Let t=u2: =∫0∞​u−1e−u2⋅2u,du=2∫0∞​e−u2,du=π​■

Gamma Distribution PDF

PDF: X∼Gamma(α,β):

f(x)=βα,Γ(α)xα−1e−x/β​,x>0

Normalization (substitution t=x/β): ∫0∞​βαΓ(α)xα−1e−x/β​,dx=Γ(α)1​∫0∞​tα−1e−t,dt=Γ(α)Γ(α)​=1■

Mean: E[X]=βαΓ(α)1​∫0∞​xαe−x/β,dx=βαΓ(α)βα+1Γ(α+1)​=β⋅α=αβ​

Variance: Var(X)=αβ2.

Special cases:

  • α=1: Exponential distribution (§6)
  • α=n/2, β=2: Chi-squared distribution with n degrees of freedom (χn2​) — fundamental in statistics and ML regularization

9. Beta Distribution

PDF: X∼Beta(α,β) on [0,1]:

f(x)=B(α,β)xα−1(1−x)β−1​,x∈[0,1]

where the Beta function is defined by requiring normalization:

B(α,β)=∫01​xα−1(1−x)β−1,dx

Key identity (proven via Gamma functions): B(α,β)=Γ(α+β)Γ(α)Γ(β)​

Mean: E[X]=B(α,β)B(α+1,β)​=Γ(α)Γ(α+β+1)Γ(α+1)Γ(α+β)​=α+βα​

Variance: Var(X)=(α+β)2(α+β+1)αβ​

Why Beta matters for ML: The Beta distribution is the conjugate prior for a Bernoulli/binomial likelihood. In Bayesian deep learning, Beta distributions appear in variational dropout, uncertainty quantification, and Thompson sampling.

Example 9.1 — Bayesian Update via Integration

Setup: A classifier’s accuracy θ∼Beta(2,2) (prior: slightly centered at 0.5). We observe 7 successes out of 10 trials. Find the posterior.

Posterior ∝ Likelihood × Prior: p(θ∣data)∝θ7(1−θ)3⋅θ2−1(1−θ)2−1=θ8(1−θ)4

This is proportional to Beta(9,5).

Posterior mean (normalizing constant found by integration): E[θ∣data]=9+59​=149​≈0.643

The normalization requires B(9,5)=∫01​θ8(1−θ)4,dθ=Γ(14)Γ(9)Γ(5)​=13!8!⋅4!​=622702080040320×24​=64351​.

10. Joint Distributions & Marginals

Definitions

For jointly distributed (X,Y) with joint PDF fX,Y​(x,y):

P((X,Y)∈A)=∬A​fX,Y​(x,y),dA

Marginal PDFs: fX​(x)=∫−∞∞​fX,Y​(x,y),dy,fY​(y)=∫−∞∞​fX,Y​(x,y),dx​

Independence: X⊥Y iff fX,Y​(x,y)=fX​(x),fY​(y) for all (x,y).

Covariance: Cov(X,Y)=E[XY]−E[X]E[Y]=∬xy,fX,Y​(x,y),dA−μX​μY​

Example 10.1 — Joint Distribution on a Triangle

Setup: (X,Y) has joint PDF f(x,y)=8xy on the region 0≤y≤x≤1 (a triangle).

Verify normalization: ∫01​∫0x​8xy,dy,dx=∫01​8x⋅2x2​,dx=∫01​4x3,dx=[x4]01​=1✓

Marginal of X: fX​(x)=∫0x​8xy,dy=8x⋅2x2​=4x3,0≤x≤1

Marginal of Y: fY​(y)=∫y1​8xy,dx=8y⋅21−y2​=4y(1−y2),0≤y≤1

E[X], E[Y]: E[X]=∫01​x⋅4x3,dx=54​,E[Y]=∫01​y⋅4y(1−y2),dy=∫01​(4y2−4y4),dy=34​−54​=158​

E[XY]: E[XY]=∫01​∫0x​8x2y2,dy,dx=∫01​38x5​,dx=38​⋅61​=94​

Cov(X,Y)=94​−54​⋅158​=94​−7532​=225100−96​=2254​>0

Positive covariance makes sense: the triangle constraint Y≤X means larger X tends to come with larger Y.

Part III — Key Theorems That Need Integrals

11. Law of the Unconscious Statistician (LOTUS)

Theorem

If Y=g(X) and X has PDF fX​, then: E[g(X)]=∫−∞∞​g(x),fX​(x),dx​

You do not need the PDF of Y to compute E[Y] — you compute directly using fX​.

Example 11.1 — Expected Squared Deviation

Setup: X∼Uniform[0,1], g(X)=(X−0.5)4. Find E[g(X)].

E[(X−0.5)4]=∫01​(x−0.5)4⋅1,dx

Let u=x−0.5: =∫−0.50.5​u4,du=2∫00.5​u4,du=2⋅5u5​​00.5​=52​⋅321​=801​​

12. Moment Generating Functions

Definition

MX​(t)=E[etX]=∫−∞∞​etx,fX​(x),dx​

Why it’s powerful: MX​(t) encodes all moments: E[Xn]=MX(n)​(0)=dtndn​MX​(t)​t=0​

Proof: MX​(t)=∫etxf(x),dx=∫∑n=0∞​n!(tx)n​f(x),dx=∑n=0∞​n!tn​E[Xn]. Differentiating n times and setting t=0 extracts E[Xn]. ■

Example 12.1 — MGF of the Normal Distribution

For X∼N(μ,σ2):

MX​(t)=∫−∞∞​etx⋅σ2π​1​e−(x−μ)2/(2σ2),dx

Complete the square in the exponent: tx−2σ2(x−μ)2​=−2σ21​[x2−2(μ+σ2t)x+μ2] =−2σ2(x−(μ+σ2t))2​+μt+2σ2t2​

Therefore: MX​(t)=eμt+σ2t2/2⋅=1 (Normal PDF integrates to 1)∫−∞∞​σ2π​1​e−(x−(μ+σ2t))2/(2σ2),dx​​

MX​(t)=eμt+σ2t2/2​

Extract moments: MX′​(t)=(μ+σ2t),eμt+σ2t2/2⟹MX′​(0)=μ=E[X]✓ MX′′​(t)=(σ2+(μ+σ2t)2),eμt+σ2t2/2⟹MX′′​(0)=σ2+μ2=E[X2]✓

13. Convolution of Independent Random Variables

Theorem

If X and Y are independent with PDFs fX​ and fY​, then Z=X+Y has PDF:

fZ​(z)=(fX​∗fY​)(z)=∫−∞∞​fX​(t),fY​(z−t),dt​

Proof: The joint PDF of (X,Y) is fX,Y​(x,y)=fX​(x)fY​(y) (by independence). The CDF of Z=X+Y: FZ​(z)=P(X+Y≤z)=∬x+y≤z​fX​(x)fY​(y),dx,dy=∫−∞∞​fX​(x)(∫−∞z−x​fY​(y),dy)dx

Differentiate with respect to z (FTC): fZ​(z)=∫−∞∞​fX​(x),fY​(z−x),dx=(fX​∗fY​)(z)■

This is the same convolution integral as signal processing (§8 of the physics note) — the mathematical structure is identical. The sum of independent random variables is the convolution of their distributions.

Example 13.1 — Sum of Two Exponentials

Setup: X,Y∼Exp(λ) independent. Find the PDF of Z=X+Y.

fZ​(z)=∫0z​λe−λt⋅λe−λ(z−t),dt=λ2e−λz∫0z​dt=λ2ze−λz,z≥0

This is the Gamma(2, 1/λ) distribution. ✓

More generally: sum of n independent Exp(λ) → Gamma(n,1/λ). The convolution integral, when applied n times, accumulates the factor from 0!z0​ to (n−1)!λnzn−1​e−λz.

Example 13.2 — Sum of Two Normals is Normal

Setup: X∼N(μ1​,σ12​), Y∼N(μ2​,σ22​) independent. Show Z=X+Y is normal.

Via MGFs (much cleaner than direct convolution): MZ​(t)=MX​(t)⋅MY​(t)=eμ1​t+σ12​t2/2⋅eμ2​t+σ22​t2/2=e(μ1​+μ2​)t+(σ12​+σ22​)t2/2

This is the MGF of N(μ1​+μ2​,,σ12​+σ22​). Since MGFs uniquely determine distributions: Z∼N(μ1​+μ2​,,σ12​+σ22​)​■

The convolution integral in closed form would require the Gaussian integral machinery — the MGF approach works because the completing-the-square calculation (Example 12.1) was done once.

14. Change of Variables — The Jacobian

Theorem (1D)

If Y=g(X) is monotone and differentiable, and X has PDF fX​:

fY​(y)=fX​(g−1(y))⋅​dyd​g−1(y)​​

Derivation: FY​(y)=P(Y≤y)=P(g(X)≤y). If g is increasing: =P(X≤g−1(y))=FX​(g−1(y)). Differentiate via chain rule: fY​(y)=fX​(g−1(y))⋅(g−1)′(y). ■

2D Theorem (MIT 18.02 L26): If (U,V)=g(X,Y): fU,V​(u,v)=fX,Y​(x(u,v),,y(u,v))⋅∣J∣ where the Jacobian: J=∂(u,v)∂(x,y)​=​∂x/∂u​∂x/∂v ∂y/∂u​∂y/∂v​​

Example 14.1 — Lognormal Distribution

Setup: X∼N(μ,σ2). Find the PDF of Y=eX (lognormal).

g(x)=ex⟹g−1(y)=lny⟹(g−1)′(y)=1/y.

fY​(y)=fX​(lny)⋅y1​=yσ2π​1​e−(lny−μ)2/(2σ2),y>0

Mean of lognormal (requires the MGF of the normal evaluated at t=1): E[Y]=E[eX]=MX​(1)=eμ+σ2/2

The eσ2/2 factor shows that the mean exceeds eμ — the log-normal is right-skewed. Used in: stock price models (Black-Scholes), income distributions, rainfall data.

Example 14.2 — Box-Muller Transform (How Computers Sample Gaussians)

Setup: U1​,U2​∼Uniform[0,1] independent. Define: Z1​=−2lnU1​​cos(2πU2​),Z2​=−2lnU1​​sin(2πU2​)

Claim: Z1​,Z2​∼N(0,1) independent.

Proof via Jacobian: Let R=−2lnU1​​, Θ=2πU2​. Then R2∼Exp(1/2) (Chi-squared with 2 df) and Θ∼Uniform[0,2π].

Joint PDF of (R,Θ): fR,Θ​(r,θ)=fR​(r)⋅fΘ​(θ)=1r​e−r2/2⋅2π1​=2πr​e−r2/2

Converting to (Z1​,Z2​)=(rcosθ,rsinθ) — polar to Cartesian: Jacobian =1/r (inverse of Cartesian-to-polar Jacobian =r):

fZ1​,Z2​​(z1​,z2​)=2πr​e−r2/2⋅r1​=2π1​e−(z12​+z22​)/2=fZ1​​2π​1​e−z12​/2​​⋅fZ2​​2π​1​e−z22​/2​​

The joint PDF factors → Z1​,Z2​ are independent N(0,1). ■

This is how every numerical library (NumPy, PyTorch, TensorFlow) generates Gaussian random numbers. Every torch.randn() call uses a variant of this Jacobian calculation.

15. Conditional Expectation as an Integral

Definition

Conditional PDF of Y given X=x: fY∣X​(y∣x)=fX​(x)fX,Y​(x,y)​

Conditional expectation: E[Y∣X=x]=∫−∞∞​y,fY∣X​(y∣x),dy

Law of Total Expectation: E[Y]=EX​[E[Y∣X]]=∫−∞∞​E[Y∣X=x],fX​(x),dx

This is a double integral — first integrate out Y at fixed x, then integrate over x. It is Fubini’s theorem in probabilistic clothing.

Example 15.1 — Regression Function

Setup: Joint PDF f(x,y)=6xy2 on 0≤x≤1, 0≤y≤1.

Marginal of X: fX​(x)=∫01​6xy2,dy=6x⋅31​=2x

Conditional PDF of Y∣X=x: fY∣X​(y∣x)=2x6xy2​=3y2,0≤y≤1

(Independent of x — Y and X are independent here.)

Conditional expectation: E[Y∣X=x]=∫01​y⋅3y2,dy=43​

The regression function is constant — as expected when X and Y are independent.

Part IV — ML & Deep Learning: Probability Integrals Everywhere

This section makes explicit what every deep learning textbook leaves implicit: the integral is the foundation.

ML.1 — Maximum Likelihood Estimation Is Integral Optimization

For i.i.d. data xi​i=1n​ from distribution pθ​, the log-likelihood:

L(θ)=∑i=1n​logpθ​(xi​)≈n∫logpθ​(x),ptrue​(x),dx

This is an expected value integral under the true distribution. MLE maximizes the expected log-likelihood — the integral over data space. For continuous models (e.g., VAEs), this expectation cannot be computed exactly and is approximated by Monte Carlo (sample average), just as in §2/§3 above.

ML.2 — Information Entropy

Shannon entropy for a continuous distribution:

H(X)=−∫−∞∞​f(x)logf(x),dx​

Gaussian entropy (derived from integration):

H(N(μ,σ2))=−∫−∞∞​f(x)logf(x),dx

=−E[−2σ2(X−μ)2​−21​log(2πσ2)]=21​+21​log(2πσ2)=21​log(2πeσ2)

(Used E[(X−μ)2]=σ2.)

Theorem: Among all continuous distributions on R with fixed mean and variance, the Gaussian maximizes entropy — proven by calculus of variations on the entropy integral. This is why the Gaussian is the “most uncertain” distribution given second-moment constraints — a fact at the heart of maximum entropy models.

ML.3 — KL Divergence: The Distance Between Distributions

DKL​(P∣Q)=∫−∞∞​p(x)logq(x)p(x)​,dx​

Non-negativity (Gibbs’ inequality) — proven by Jensen’s inequality applied to the integral:

DKL​(P∣Q)=−∫p(x)logp(x)q(x)​,dx≥−log∫p(x)⋅p(x)q(x)​,dx=−log1=0

KL between two Gaussians (closed form from evaluating the integral):

DKL​(N(μ1​,σ12​)∣N(μ2​,σ22​))=logσ1​σ2​​+2σ22​σ12​+(μ1​−μ2​)2​−21​

This appears in VAE loss functions as the regularization term, forcing the encoder to match a standard Gaussian prior. The entire VAE training objective is:

L=reconstruction: ∫logpθ​⋅qϕ​,dzEqϕ​(z∣x)​[logpθ​(x∣z)]​​−two Gaussian integralsDKL​(qϕ​(z∣x)∣p(z))​​

Both terms are integrals.

ML.4 — The Evidence Lower Bound (ELBO) is an Integral

In Variational Inference, we want logp(x) but it requires an intractable integral:

logp(x)=log∫p(x∣z),p(z),dz

We lower bound it (Jensen’s inequality on the integral):

logp(x)≥∫q(z)logq(z)p(x,z)​,dz=:ELBO(q)

The ELBO is a functional of q — optimizing over it is variational calculus applied to integrals. This is the mathematical core of:

  • Variational Autoencoders (VAEs)
  • Bayesian Neural Networks
  • Diffusion Models (score matching is related)

ML.5 — Monte Carlo Integration: SGD as Approximate Integration

Problem: I=∫X​f(x),p(x),dx=Ep​[f(X)]

Monte Carlo estimate: I^n​=n1​∑i=1n​f(xi​), xi​∼p.

Strong Law: I^n​→I almost surely (law of large numbers).

Rate of convergence (Central Limit Theorem): n​(I^n​−I)d​N(0,Varp​[f(X)])

Error ∼O(1/n​), independent of dimension. This is why Monte Carlo is preferred over numerical quadrature in high dimensions (quadrature error degrades exponentially with dimension — the “curse of dimensionality”).

SGD is mini-batch Monte Carlo integration of the gradient:

∇θ​L=∫∇θ​ℓ(fθ​(x),y),p(x,y),dx,dy≈B1​∑i∈batch​∇θ​ℓ(fθ​(xi​),yi​)

Every SGD step is an unbiased Monte Carlo estimate of the true gradient integral.

ML.6 — The Reparameterization Trick: Differentiating Through an Integral

Problem: In a VAE, the encoder outputs qϕ​(z∣x)=N(μϕ​,σϕ2​) and we need:

∇ϕ​Eqϕ​​[f(z)]=∇ϕ​∫f(z),qϕ​(z∣x),dz

Naive Monte Carlo can’t differentiate through the sampling step.

Reparameterization: Write z=μϕ​+σϕ​ε, ε∼N(0,1):

∫f(z),qϕ​(z∣x),dz=∫f(μϕ​+σϕ​ε),ϕ(ε),dε

Now ϕ(ε) is independent of ϕ, so we can move ∇ϕ​ inside the integral:

∇ϕ​∫f(μϕ​+σϕ​ε),ϕ(ε),dε=∫∇ϕ​f(μϕ​+σϕ​ε),ϕ(ε),dε

This is the Leibniz rule (differentiation under the integral sign), applied to make backpropagation through stochastic layers possible. Without this, VAEs cannot be trained.

Leibniz Rule (used here): dαd​∫ab​f(x,α),dx=∫ab​∂α∂f​(x,α),dx

(valid when ∂f/∂α is continuous and bounds a,b are independent of α.)

ML.7 — Score Function & Fisher Information

The score function is: s(x;θ)=∇θ​logpθ​(x)

Fisher Information Matrix: I(θ)=E[s(x;θ)s(x;θ)T]=∫∇θ​logpθ​(x),(∇θ​logpθ​(x))T,pθ​(x),dx

This is an integral of an outer product — a matrix-valued integral. It appears in:

  • Natural Gradient descent (K-FAC optimizer)
  • Score matching (diffusion models)
  • Cramér-Rao bound (fundamental lower bound on variance of any estimator)

Cramér-Rao Bound: Var(θ^)≥I(θ)−1

The bound is an integral inequality — proven by applying Cauchy-Schwarz to the integral ∫s(x;θ),pθ​(x),dx.

(PDF normalization)∫−∞∞​f(x),dx=1

(Probability)P(a≤X≤b)=∫ab​f(x),dx

(CDF)F(x)=∫−∞x​f(t),dt,f(x)=F′(x)

(Mean)μ=E[X]=∫−∞∞​x,f(x),dx

(LOTUS)E[g(X)]=∫−∞∞​g(x),f(x),dx

(Variance)σ2=E[X2]−μ2=∫x2f(x),dx−(∫x,f(x),dx)2

(Joint → Marginal)fX​(x)=∫−∞∞​fX,Y​(x,y),dy

(Convolution)fX+Y​(z)=∫−∞∞​fX​(t),fY​(z−t),dt

(Change of variables)fY​(y)=fX​(g−1(y))​dyd​g−1(y)​

(MGF)MX​(t)=E[etX]=∫etxf(x),dx

(Entropy)H(X)=−∫f(x)logf(x),dx

(KL divergence)DKL​(P∣Q)=∫p(x)logq(x)p(x)​,dx

(Gaussian integral)∫−∞∞​e−x2,dx=π​,∫−∞∞​e−x2/(2σ2),dx=σ2π​

(Gamma function)Γ(n)=∫0∞​tn−1e−t,dt=(n−1)!,Γ(1/2)=π​
